title: In Defense of Loneliness: The Adaptive Functions of a Misunderstood State.
abstract: Loneliness is often portrayed as a public-health threat, yet this framing obscures important distinctions and empirical evidence that have been provided by different psychological frameworks. Although chronic loneliness-especially when paired with social isolation-is linked to impaired social functioning and psychiatric risk, acute loneliness may serve an adaptive role. Evidence suggests that acute loneliness can, in fact, enhance social attention, affiliative motivation, and readiness for interpersonal synchrony and may foster introspection and social cognition. Loneliness, therefore, is not inherently pathological, and differentiating acute from chronic loneliness appears essential for clinical practice and public discourse. In this article, I challenge the deficit-based framing of loneliness by providing a brief synthesis of some of the relevant psychological, relational, and clinical frameworks.
